M1.topicAr: Phishing and checking messages and links

M2.topicAr: Passwords, sign-in checks and verification codes

M1.C1.feedbackAr: Don't tap a link you got in a message or send your details in reply. Open the official app yourself and check there.
M1.C1.hintAr: Where did the link come from? The safe path starts from the app you open yourself.

M1.C2.feedbackAr: Your friend's account may be stolen. Before opening any strange link, ask them another way: did you send this?
M1.C2.hintAr: Does your friend usually write this way? How do you know it's them?

M1.C3.feedbackAr: The lock in the address bar and a polished look don't prove a site is real. Look at the address itself and what it asks of you.
M1.C3.hintAr: A scammer can make a lock and a logo. What can't they copy?

M2.C1.feedbackAr: Give each account a long password you use nowhere else, and let a password manager remember it for you.
M2.C1.hintAr: If one password is stolen, how many accounts open?

M2.C2.labelAr: Who is asking for the code?
M2.C2.feedbackAr: Only you type the verification code, in the app you opened yourself to sign in. Never send it to anyone who asks, whatever they say.
M2.C2.hintAr: The code is your account's key. Who needs your key but you?

M2.C3.feedbackAr: Two-step verification is your account's second lock: even with your password, no one gets in without the code. Turn it on for every important account.
M2.C3.hintAr: A password is one lock. What if the door had two?

M3.C1.labelAr: Where do I download the game?
M3.C1.feedbackAr: Download apps and games only from the official store. “Free” and “modded” copies from links often carry harmful programs.
M3.C1.hintAr: Who checks apps before they reach you?

M3.C2.feedbackAr: Ask: does the app need this permission to do its job? If not, deny it. An extra permission is a door to your data.
M3.C2.hintAr: What is the app's job? Is what it asks for related to it?

M3.C3.feedbackAr: Don't turn off your device's protection or allow installs from unknown sources. A trusted app never asks you to.
M3.C3.hintAr: Why does it want you to turn off protection first?

M4.C1.feedbackAr: Updates close holes attackers use. Install them without long delay, and only from device settings or the official store.
M4.C1.hintAr: An update fixes a hole. What happens if it stays open?

M4.C2.feedbackAr: Keep a second copy of your important files somewhere other than the device itself, and try restoring a file once to be sure it works.
M4.C2.hintAr: If the device broke today, where would your files be?

M4.C3.labelAr: Locked files and a ransom demand
M4.C3.feedbackAr: Don't pay the blackmailer or download what they send. Tell an adult you trust, and restore your files from the backup.
M4.C3.hintAr: You have a backup. Do you even need what the blackmailer offers?

M5.C1.labelAr: A sign-in attempt on your account
M5.C1.feedbackAr: If it isn't you trying to sign in, tap “Deny”, then change your password: the alert means someone knows it.
M5.C1.hintAr: You didn't try to sign in. So who is trying?

M5.C2.feedbackAr: Whoever rushes you doesn't want you to think. Stop, check in the official app yourself, and don't do what the message says, not even half.
M5.C2.hintAr: Why do they want you to act “now”?

M5.C3.labelAr: After a mistake: what do I do?
M5.C3.feedbackAr: Mistakes happen to anyone. What matters is acting fast: change your password right away and tell an adult you trust. Hiding it makes the harm worse.
M5.C3.hintAr: Time matters after a mistake. What stops the scammer now?
